title: 2nd Week: 21 to 25 of september
text:
Investigate other tools
I investigated other options to perform the analysis of the samples. First I read about StarDist, that use image-mask pairs cropped from the original image into different regions (128x128) to train a model (split into test and train). Also it raises the option of doing data augmentation by geometrically distorting the input images.
Also, I read about SMURF and started writing a script for when we finish with SpaceRanger, beacuse the SR outputs are the SMURF inputs.

title: 2nd Week: 21 to 25 of september
text:
SMURF
One of the doubts that I had about SMURF is the third input explained in the SMURF manual, ‘segmentation_final.npy’. As indicated it is generated by performing your own segmentation over so.image_temp(), resulting in a NumPy array with the shape as so.image_temp().
I think the .npy file comes from StarDist segmentation –> I’m not sure of this beacuse in the documentation they don’t mention explicitly the outputs, although they mention:
“The image annotations (also known as label images or label masks) should be integer-valued (e.g. 8-bit, 16-bit, 32-bit) TIFF files where all background pixels have value 0 and each object instance is represented by an area/volume filled with a unique positive integer value. It does not matter what the values are and they do not need to be consecutive. Please note that a foreground/background segmentation mask, where all object instances are denoted by the same value, is not sufficient for StarDist training.”
I think this is basicly what SMURF needs.
SpaceRanger does not generate any NumPy array, the only file that could supply this input is the nucleus_instance_mask.tiff. So, I searched how to convert a tiff file to a numpy array and I found the following code:
import tifffile

tiff_image = tiff.imread('smurf_segmentation/outs/nucleus_instance_mask.tiff')
array_image = np.array(tiff_image)
Now I have to check if effectively the .tiff file generated by SpaceRanger is compatible with the input of SMURF.

title: 2nd Week: 21 to 25 of september
text:
TMA_7_8
Ele sent us an excel with the info. about the quality of each sample (saturation, presence of tumor, histology, etc.), and taking it into account we decided to start analyzing the samples 7_8. They were both classified as “bien”, with high seq_saturation and “OK” for hystology-annotation but low UMIs (we will see how this affect to the results).
Then the same process as we did with the sample 3_4 was followed this time (aligning cytassist+image, online SR..) but first I convert the original image into a pyramidal one, to make it compatible with SR (ome.tif).
After 2h we obtained the results and summing up they are worse than what we obtained with samples 3 and 4. The total UMIs in cells are about a 12%. Also, we noticed that the quality of the image decreased a lot in comparison with what we see when we load the image (ome.tif) in QuPath.
To check this I would try to see if just the image with the segmentation is an output of SR, to confirm if this lower quality is only because of the report .html format. If the quality is bad in both images, the individual and the added to the report, then we would have to study if using SR in the cloud is not obtaining good results because of the way it process the image.

first_channel = '0' # @param ['None', 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
second_channel = '1' # @param ['None', 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
third_channel = '2' # @param ['None', 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

selected_channels = []
for i, c in enumerate([first_channel, second_channel, third_channel]):
  if c == 'None':
    continue
  if int(c) > img.shape[-1]:
    assert False, 'invalid channel index, must have index greater or equal to the number of channels'
  if c != 'None':
    selected_channels.append(int(c))

img_selected_channels = np.zeros_like(img)
img_selected_channels[:, :, :len(selected_channels)] = img[:, :, selected_channels]

flow_threshold = 0.4
cellprob_threshold = 0.0
